source.title: Parallel-SFT: Improving Zero-Shot Cross-Programming-Language Transfer for Code RL
source.authors: Zhaofeng Wu; Shi-Qi Wang; Bo Peng; A. Goyal; Melanie Kambadur; Sebastian Ruder; Yoon Kim; Chloe Bi

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures similarity between representations of equivalent programs in different programming languages, using retrieval accuracy and adjusted cosine similarity. This conceptually tests cross-language representation alignment, but in code rather than the claim’s vision-language setting.
record.gate_note: The paper’s RL transfer and code-task performance results are not rows because they measure task performance, not representation alignment. The representation analysis reports layer-wise curves for three SFT mixtures and two similarity measures; plotted values are not stated numerically in the text.
record.test_reason: The study measures how closely one model (Llama-3.1-8B after different SFT mixtures) places translations of the same program in Go, PHP and Ruby. That is within-model cross-language alignment of inputs. It is not convergence between independently trained models, across modalities or across seeds, and it tests no mapping between models. The strongest effect comes from Parallel-SFT, which is built to induce the alignment. The paper cites the Platonic Representation Hypothesis in §4, arguing that natural languages share an 'underlying reality' while programming languages are domain-specialized. It argues this but does not test it, so the finding belongs under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that non-parallel multi-PL SFT improves alignment of equivalent programs across unseen PLs and that Parallel-SFT improves it further, giving a more functionality-centric latent space. They hypothesize, without testing directly, that this contributes to better zero-shot cross-PL RL transfer. They also argue that programming languages lack the shared grounding in 'underlying reality' that natural languages have, citing Huh et al.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses cross-program alignment measured by retrieval accuracy and adjusted cosine similarity, not a scale sweep of similarities between independently trained models. Its comparison varies SFT data mixtures within an 8B model; it also examines layer-wise patterns.
record.method_sensitivity: Representation alignment varies by layer: both metrics follow an inverted-U profile, peaking in intermediate layers. Adjusted cosine similarity for the parallel mixture is described as similar to baseline at the two ends and higher in the middle.

fits_no_version.finding: Within one Llama-3.1-8B model, cross-programming-language alignment of equivalent programs rises with multi-PL SFT and further with parallel-program SFT. This holds on both retrieval accuracy and adjusted cosine similarity, with an inverted-U profile across layers peaking in middle layers (Fig. 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-model cross-language (cross-PL) representation alignment depends on training-data composition, especially explicit parallel data, and peaks in intermediate layers.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The representation results are shown only in plots, without numerical values stated in the text. The representation analysis uses 312 held-out programs and three target programming languages; it does not test model scaling or generality across architectures.
record.rows_left_out: None. The RL transfer and code-task results were not included because they measure task performance rather than representation alignment.

untested.parts: No comparison across independently trained models, architectures or scale.
No vision or language pairing; code only.
No mapping or stitching between models.
The layer and metric dependence shown concerns within-model cross-PL alignment, not between-model convergence.
The study does not measure convergence between models, so the role of shared data in it is untested. The §4 argument about shared reality is discussion only.

record.verdict_notes: The main results are RL transfer performance, which are correctly excluded from the rows. The record's V6 and V7 labels were removed because the measured construct is within-model alignment of translated inputs, not convergence between models. The record did not mention that Huh et al. is cited in §4 as an argument, which is why the relation is 'discusses'.

versions.untested_parts: No scale sweep, increase in model capability, or comparison across architectures, objectives, and data sources as models grow.
No vision-language models or paired images and captions; the study examines programming languages.
No comparison across random initializations of the same architecture, and no test of shared features or subspaces across seeds.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
The study varies layer and reports two similarity metrics, but does not test other neighbour settings or out-of-distribution inputs.

The study compares SFT data mixtures and reports similarity of held-out equivalent programs across programming languages. It does not establish a scale-related plateau or test whether a common model of reality explains alignment.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B base + 1 Language SFT
rows.operation_detail: Measured alignment of held-out parallel program representations across layers.

conditions.value: Go, PHP, Ruby; unseen during SFT

rows.measure: Whether each program representation is closer to its translation than to noncorresponding programs.
rows.note: The text reports that both multi-language mixtures improve alignment over this monolingual baseline, but does not state this baseline’s numerical values. The plotted curve is described as having an inverted-U layer profile.
rows.check: Measures within-model cross-PL alignment, not convergence between models. This is the 1 Language baseline curve, figure only.

rows.operation_detail: Measured alignment of held-out parallel program representations across layers.

conditions.value: Go, PHP, Ruby; unseen during SFT

rows.measure: Whether each program representation is closer to its translation than to noncorresponding programs.
rows.value: figure only; text states alignment improves over the monolingual baseline
rows.note: The text describes improved alignment over the monolingual baseline and an inverted-U pattern across layers; plotted values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: Different construct (within-model cross-PL alignment). The rise over the 1 Language mixture is stated in the text; values are figure only.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B base + 8 Languages (parallel) SFT
rows.operation_detail: Measured alignment of held-out parallel program representations across layers.

conditions.value: Go, PHP, Ruby; unseen during SFT

rows.measure: Whether each program representation is closer to its translation than to noncorresponding programs.
rows.value: figure only; text states explicit parallel-program training further improves alignment
rows.note: The text reports that parallel training further improves alignment beyond non-parallel multi-language training. The plotted curve is described as having an inverted-U layer profile.
rows.check: Different construct. The SFT mixture is designed to induce alignment, so the increase is engineered rather than emergent.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B base + 1 Language SFT
rows.operation_detail: Measured adjusted cosine similarity of held-out parallel program representations across layers.

conditions.value: Go, PHP, Ruby; unseen during SFT

rows.measure: Cosine similarity of corresponding program representations minus the estimated similarity of non-parallel pairs.
rows.note: The text describes the multi-language mixtures as improving alignment over this baseline. It specifically says parallel-SFT adjusted cosine similarities are similar to baseline at the two ends and higher in middle layers; the plotted baseline values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: Baseline curve for adjusted cosine similarity, figure only. Different construct.

rows.operation_detail: Measured adjusted cosine similarity of held-out parallel program representations across layers.

conditions.value: Go, PHP, Ruby; unseen during SFT

rows.measure: Cosine similarity of corresponding program representations minus the estimated similarity of non-parallel pairs.
rows.value: figure only; text states non-parallel multi-PL training improves alignment over the monolingual baseline
rows.note: The text describes an inverted-U pattern across layers. Values are presented only in the plot.
rows.check: Different construct. The rise over baseline is stated in text only.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B base + 8 Languages (parallel) SFT
rows.operation_detail: Measured adjusted cosine similarity of held-out parallel program representations across layers.

conditions.value: Go, PHP, Ruby; unseen during SFT

rows.measure: Cosine similarity of corresponding program representations minus the estimated similarity of non-parallel pairs.
rows.value: figure only; text states similarity is notably higher in middle layers and similar to baseline at the two ends
rows.note: The text says parallel-SFT accentuates the inverted-U layer pattern: the middle layers show higher alignment, while the two ends are similar to baseline.
rows.check: Different construct. 'Partial' was misapplied: the text says alignment is higher than baseline in middle layers and similar at the ends, which is a layer profile, not a weak effect. It is the highest of the three mixtures.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: All three SFT mixtures across the tested layers
reader_labels.reason: Both similarity measures show an inverted-U layer profile, with alignment higher in intermediate layers and lower at the ends; for adjusted cosine, parallel-SFT is described as similar to baseline at the two ends. This shows layer choice matters (R1–R6).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Held-out equivalent programs across Go, PHP, and Ruby after the tested SFT mixtures
reader_labels.reason: The text reports greater alignment after non-parallel multi-language SFT than after monolingual SFT, and further improvement after explicit parallel-program SFT, supporting a role for training data and explicit alignment signals (R2, R3, R5, R6).
